terms.definition: A command-line program used to create, view, and modify text files in a Linux terminal without a graphical interface
terms.example: Like Notepad for Windows, but for the Linux command line

terms.definition: A beginner-friendly command-line text editor that displays available shortcuts at the bottom of the screen
terms.example: nano report.txt opens or creates report.txt for editing

terms.definition: Visual Editor — the original screen-based Unix text editor, standard on every POSIX-compliant Linux system
terms.example: vi config.txt opens config.txt; available on every Linux server including EC2 instances

terms.definition: Vi IMproved — an enhanced version of vi with syntax highlighting, multi-level undo, and plugins while maintaining vi compatibility
terms.example: vim script.sh is used exactly like vi but with extra features

terms.definition: The default mode in vi/vim when a file opens — used for navigation, deletion, copying, and entering other modes; you cannot type text here
terms.example: Press Esc from any mode to return to Command Mode

terms.definition: The vi/vim mode where you can freely type and edit text; entered by pressing i, a, or o from Command Mode
terms.example: Press i in Command Mode — the -- INSERT -- indicator appears at the bottom

terms.definition: Also called Ex Mode — the vi/vim mode used for commands like saving (:w), quitting (:q), and searching; entered by pressing : from Command Mode
terms.example: Type :wq in Last Line Mode to save and quit the file

terms.definition: The vi/vim command in Last Line Mode to save (write) the file and then quit the editor
terms.example: Esc → :wq → Enter saves all changes and exits vi

terms.definition: The vi/vim command to force-quit without saving any changes; the ! overrides the safety check
terms.example: Use :q! when you want to discard changes and exit immediately

terms.definition: Word Count — a Linux command that counts lines, words, and characters in a file
terms.example: wc report.txt shows: 10 50 300 report.txt (10 lines, 50 words, 300 chars)

terms.definition: Global Regular Expression Print — a command that searches for a pattern inside files and prints matching lines
terms.example: grep 'error' /var/log/syslog finds all lines containing the word error

terms.definition: Case-insensitive grep — matches the search term regardless of uppercase or lowercase letters
terms.example: grep -i 'error' syslog matches 'error', 'Error', and 'ERROR'

terms.definition: Recursive grep — searches through all files inside a directory and all its subdirectories
terms.example: grep -r 'TODO' ~/projects searches every file in the projects folder

terms.definition: Grep with line numbers — shows the line number alongside each matching line for easy location
terms.example: grep -n 'error' app.log shows: 42: error connecting to database

terms.definition: A Linux command that sorts lines in a file alphabetically (default), numerically, or in reverse order
terms.example: sort names.txt displays names in A-Z order without modifying the file

terms.definition: Numeric sort — sorts lines by their numeric value rather than alphabetically
terms.example: sort -n numbers.txt sorts 1, 2, 10, 20 correctly (vs alphabetical which gives 1, 10, 2, 20)

terms.definition: Reverse sort — reverses the sort order, giving Z-A alphabetically or 9-0 numerically when combined with -n
terms.example: sort -r names.txt gives reverse alphabetical; sort -nr numbers.txt gives largest-first

terms.definition: Unique sort — sorts the file and removes duplicate lines from the output
terms.example: sort -u fruits.txt with duplicate 'apple' entries shows 'apple' only once

terms.definition: The | character in Linux that takes the output of one command and feeds it as input to the next command, chaining multiple commands together
terms.example: grep 'error' syslog | wc -l counts error lines by combining grep and wc

terms.definition: Portable Operating System Interface — a standard that defines how Unix/Linux systems must behave; vi is POSIX standard and therefore available on every compliant system
terms.example: Because vi is POSIX standard, it is pre-installed on every Linux server including AWS EC2 instances

terms.definition: A property of Linux commands where uppercase and lowercase letters are treated as completely different characters
terms.example: 'nano' is a valid command but 'Nano' or 'NANO' will produce a 'command not found' error

terms.definition: The wc option that counts only the number of lines in a file
terms.example: wc -l /var/log/syslog quickly tells you how many log entries exist

terms.definition: The wc option that counts only the number of words in a file
terms.example: wc -w essay.txt tells you the word count of your document

terms.definition: The wc option that counts only the number of characters (bytes) in a file
terms.example: wc -c config.txt shows the exact byte size of the file
